chapter_theme: The merchant Subhadran reads the auspicious marks on Civakan's body, decides he is his daughter's destined husband and brings him home; a hymn to the Jina is sung as they enter, Kemasari and Civakan fall in love at first sight, the house bathes and feasts him, and he lies lamenting the wounds of her beauty.

cast.role: the hero, a stranger arriving at Kemamapuram, read by the merchant as Kemasari's destined husband; called காளை, வள்ளல், செல்வன் here
the wealthy merchant of Kemamapuram, Kemasari's father (named at 1450), who reads Civakan's bodily marks and takes him home
Subhadran's daughter, destined to marry the man at whose sight she feels shy
the unnamed woman who garlands her vina and sings the hymn to the Jina as the chariot passes (1466-1469); possibly Kemasari
the unnamed woman likened to Rambha who hears the hymn and blesses the girl with a fitting husband (1470)
the women of Subhadran's house who bathe, dress and feed Civakan

1461.reading: The catalogue of the stranger's body goes on: his limbs are full and handsome, his neck is fit to be seen like a sounding gem drum, and his mouth has the colour of a fierce great tiger's.
1461.nuance: This continues the head-to-foot survey begun at 1460 as the merchant looks the stranger over; each part is measured against a standard object, as a reader of bodily signs would measure it.

1462.reading: On his hill-broad chest there are three lines, his tongue is flawless and gold-like, his shoulders are like hills, and his arms have the shape of the trunk of the king of the gods' elephant.
1462.nuance: The three lines on the chest (வரியு மூன்று) and the elephant-trunk arms are marks to be read, not only praised: they are the kind of signs that let a father decide whom to give his daughter to (1465).

1463.reading: The navel of this prince, who is like a shining golden hill, is like the seed-pod of a petalled lotus, deep and whorled to the right, and gives off a sweet scent.
1463.nuance: The rightward whorl (வலஞ்சுழி) is the auspicious turn, as of the right-whorled conch; the description reads the body as a set of good omens.

1464.reading: His wrists are thick and fitted to their measure, his calves outdo the kediru fish in beauty, his fingers are so close that not even a mustard seed can pass between them, and his nose is like a goad set with a rare gem.
1464.nuance: Fingers that leave no gap (கடிப்பகை நுழைவற) are a sign of a hand that holds wealth; the survey keeps to the signs a merchant would value.

1465.reading: Seeing a mouth set with long shining teeth like coral, and palms and feet like lotuses, the merchant concluded that this was the husband of Tirumagal, settled it, spoke with him and took him up onto his chariot.
1465.event: Subhadran, having read the marks on Civakan's body, decides he is the destined husband, speaks with him and takes him onto his chariot.
1465.nuance: திருமகள் கணவன் can be heard two ways: Lakshmi's lord, a man of royal fortune, and the husband of the merchant's own daughter, whom the house has been waiting for (1453 calls him திருமகன்). The decision is made by reading the body, not by asking the stranger's birth.

1466.reading: As they rode the chariot, a creeper-like woman took a lovely garland, set it on her great-sounding vina, plucked with her sharp nail and sang of the god the world knows.
1466.event: As Subhadran and Civakan ride in, a woman garlands her vina and begins a hymn to the Jina.
1466.nuance: The text does not name the singer; she may be Kemasari herself or a woman of the house. Garlanding the instrument before playing is a worship of the vina.

1467.reading: The singer says that those who do not scatter honeyed flowers and praise with their tongues the lord of the gods, sea-coloured, under the three umbrellas beneath the fragrant flowering pindi tree, will not reach the world of release.

claims.claim: those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and the tongue do not reach the world of release

1467.nuance: The pindi (asoka) tree and the triple umbrella mark the Jina. The repeated half-line (தேவர் பெருமானைத் தேவர் பெருமானை) is the refrain form of a sung hymn, kept in all three stanzas.

1468.reading: She sings that the sea-coloured one under the three umbrellas, lord of those who rose by slaying the mighty five senses, knew without flaw, and that those who do not sing his lotus feet without stain will not reach the world of the gods.

claims.claim: the Jina conquered the five senses and knows without flaw
those who do not sing the Jina's feet do not reach heaven

1468.nuance: The refrain shifts from வீட்டுலகம் (1467, 1469) to வானுலகம் here: release and the heaven of the gods are not the same goal in Jain teaching, and the hymn names both as the reward of praise. காசின்று உணர்ந்தான் points to the Jina's faultless knowing.

1469.reading: Those who do not praise, until their tongues are calloused, the sea-coloured one beneath the ever-flowering pindi will not reach the world of release; the thieves that are their deeds waylay them, and their souls, their eight qualities seized, are driven off.

claims.claim: karma waylays the soul like a robber and takes its eight qualities
those who do not praise the Jina do not reach release

1469.nuance: On my reading of கோட்பட்டு, the eight qualities (எண்குணன்) here belong to the souls, plundered by deeds pictured as highway robbers (வினைக்கள்வர் ஆறலைப்ப), in keeping with the Jain teaching of eight karmas that cover the soul's eight qualities. The line is compressed and the construction is not certain.

1470.reading: Hearing her sing the feet of the pearl-sea-coloured one whom the three worlds sing with devotion, a woman like Rambha rejoiced and said, 'May she now win a man of skill fit to match her.'
1470.event: A woman who hears the hymn blesses the girl with a fitting husband, just as Civakan arrives.
1470.nuance: The wish is spoken as the destined husband enters the city, so it works as an auspicious word heard at the right moment. Who speaks and who இவள் is (the singer, or Kemasari) is not clear from the verse alone.

1471.reading: When they entered the long city, where treasure lay so thick the ground seemed to eat it, the gaze of the girl like a shining flowering creeper and the gaze of the man with mighty shoulders met as one.
1471.event: As Civakan enters the city with Subhadran, he and Kemasari see each other and their eyes meet.
1471.nuance: நோக்கும் ஒத்த: the two looks are equal and simultaneous, the first-sight meeting of Tamil love poetry.

1472.reading: On seeing the young man, her bangles slipped down to the ground, her fair colour, her inner restraint and her modesty all broke, and desire kindled a bright fire in which she melted.
1472.event: At the sight of Civakan, Kemasari is overcome with desire.
1472.nuance: The signs of a separated woman's wasting (slipping bangles, lost colour) come here at the first instant of sight, before any separation.

1473.reading: He who was master of the vina, whose lute was a goddess of speech, was pained as her glance became an afflicting goddess and sickened his mind; wondering whether she was a striking goddess or a mortal daughter, he sank down.
1473.event: Struck by Kemasari's look, Civakan wonders whether she is a goddess or a woman and is overcome.
1473.nuance: The word play runs on அணங்கு three times: வாக்கணங்கு (the lute as the goddess of speech), நோக்கணங்கு (her look as the goddess that afflicts), தாக்கணங்கு (the goddess who strikes). The vina-master who won Gandharvadattai by sound is here undone by sight.

1474.reading: Saying that their mistress, whose face shamed the lotus and whose eyes were like killing spears, had melted, her companions spread the word and came and gathered round the strong-chested man.
1474.event: Kemasari's companions see she is in love and crowd round Civakan.
1474.nuance: The companions read her state from her body and act on it at once, the friend's role of Tamil love poetry turned into a crowd.

1475.reading: Gazing at the beauty of the man of merit, like a bull among the herd, as if she had reached a long, full bliss beyond thought, the field-creeper girl with her grace looked once on his loveliness and turned her sword-like eyes away.
1475.event: Kemasari looks at Civakan in rapture and then turns her eyes away.
1475.nuance: நிப்புதி is a rare word; it seems to be a loan of Prakrit nivvui (nirvrti), the bliss of release, used here as a simile for the joy of a lover's gaze. Turning her eyes away (வாட்கண் அகன்றாள்) is the shyness the astrologer named as the sign of the destined husband (1451).

1476.reading: They anointed the generous man with scented oil, bathed him with clear water poured from jewelled pots, dressed him in cloth that had drunk in sweet incense, and adorned him with a honey-dripping garland and ornaments.
1476.event: The women of the house bathe Civakan, dress him and adorn him.

1477.reading: After they had wiped on the auspicious white paste and drawn the pearls into place, the women with fragrant garlands took him inside and brought nectar-like food in bright golden vessels, and he ate it in proper style.
1477.event: The women lead Civakan in and serve him food in golden vessels, and he eats.
1477.nuance: மங்கல வெள்ளை and முத்து ஈர்த்த are hard to fix; the sense of the second half, the meal, is clear.

1478.reading: Seated on a painted cushion upon a golden platform set with inlay rows, so that his dignity was honoured, the garlanded lord rinsed with water from a pitcher like pearl and gem and finished that rite.
1478.event: Civakan washes after the meal, seated on a cushion on a golden platform.

1479.reading: The areca pieces, scented with plump fruit and fragrant spice, came in a golden betel bag of Yavana workmanship, with crystal split and set, gold inlaid at its edges and pearls pressed along the rim.
1479.event: Betel and areca are brought to Civakan in a jewelled bag.
1479.nuance: The Yavana craftsmanship (யவனக் கைவினை) marks the merchant house as rich in foreign goods.

1480.reading: He rolled the green leaves, chewed them, wiped his teeth till they shone, spat, and took the sweet fragrance into his mouth, while his gem earrings swung and shot their light aside, as they say.
1480.event: Civakan chews betel after the meal.

1481.reading: Civakan says: her girdle and fine cloth, spread over the broad hips of the girl whose speech is melody, pour out a fresh light from within and have captured the eyes and heart of wretched me.
1481.nuance: The lament begins after the feast: the guest has been honoured in every way and is alone with longing. பாவியேன் is the lover's self-pity, not a confession of sin.

1482.reading: He says the cruel girl binds his whole body with her fragrant hair, beats him with the strong bow of her brows bent at the middle, and, before her long flower eyes have even split his life, her young breasts kill and kill again.
1482.nuance: Each feature is a weapon in a sequence of capture and execution: hair the rope, brow the bow, eyes the blade, breasts the death stroke. The doubled கொல்லும் is the climax.

1483.reading: He says her hot breasts, cruel enough to be bound by a bodice, smeared with saffron, spread over with pearls on their sloping ground, destroy even the ground of her waist; what will they not do to me?
1483.nuance: The bodice (கச்சு) is described as a restraint put on something dangerous, which the next verse repeats for the hair.

1484.reading: He says her flower-decked hair, dark and fragrant within, is bound and coiled and thrown behind her; if it is like that, what will it not do? It bewilders like her large eyes, which are long and red-lined.
1484.nuance: கட்டப் பட்டன is repeated from 1483: hair and breasts are both things that had to be bound, and still they overpower him.

links.note: 1453 tells how the merchant fed 1008 people daily for twelve years for the sake of the திருமகன் who would be his daughter's husband; in 1465 he reads the stranger's body and names him திருமகள் கணவன்.
links.teaches: The twelve years of feeding were a long wait for a sign, and the sign comes as a body to be read, so the epic turns the merchant's charity into the means by which the fated groom is found.

links.note: In 1339 Padumai's royal father gives her because Civakan bears marks fit to rule the earth (பொறியினன்); in 1465 the merchant Subhadran gives his consent on the same kind of reading of the body.
links.teaches: Two fathers of different rank, a king and a merchant, both choose the stranger by reading his body rather than asking his birth, which shows that in the epic the hero's hidden royalty is legible on his skin to anyone trained to look.

links.note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face; Subhadran, who has kept a great guest-feeding for years (1451, 1453), receives a guest he calls திருமகள் கணவன்.
links.teaches: The Kural's promise that fortune lives in the hospitable house is made literal: the guest the merchant takes in is the lord of fortune himself and becomes the son of the house.

gains.a: a reason, in the ethics of hospitality, why the long feeding is rewarded by the arrival of Tirumagal's husband
gains.b: a story in which the goddess's dwelling in the host's house arrives as a person, a guest who joins the family

links.note: Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot cross the sea of births; 1467 says those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and tongue do not reach the world of release.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves the Lord unnamed and the means as reaching his feet; the Jain hymn names him by the pindi tree and the triple umbrella and makes the condition a concrete act of worship, so the same exclusion becomes sectarian and ritual.

gains.a: the general frame of the couplet, which shows that the hymn's threat belongs to a shared Tamil form of praise
gains.b: an instance of how a Jain reader could fill the Kural's unnamed Lord with the Jina and its reaching with flowers and song

links.note: Kural 6 praises the one who quenched the five gates of sense (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep his path; 1468 calls the Jina lord of those who slew the five senses (ஐம்பொறியும் அட்டு) and promises heaven to those who sing his feet.
links.teaches: The Kural's sense-quencher is a teacher whose path is followed; in the hymn he is the head of a class of victors, and the reward moves from long life on earth to the world of the gods.

gains.a: a named model for the Jina's epithet, which shows the hymn speaking the Kural's language of sense-conquest
gains.b: evidence that the couplet's sense-quencher was read in Jain circles as the Jina and his followers

links.note: In Tirumanthiram 1775 worship of the Lord's feet brings grace by which the worshipper's own five senses are conquered; in 1468 the Jina conquered his own senses, and the worshipper's singing earns heaven, not sense-conquest.
links.teaches: Both tie the five senses to praise of holy feet, but the conquest is done by different hands: Saiva grace subdues the devotee's senses for him, while in the Jain hymn the conquest belongs to the Jina alone and remains the worshipper's own task.

gains.a: a contrast that shows the hymn gives the worshipper no grace that does the work of restraint
gains.b: a Jain counterpart in which the feet are praised for a conquest already achieved by their owner, not for one they bestow

links.note: Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், the one of eight qualities, and calls a head that does not bow useless; in 1469 those who do not praise the Jina have the eight qualities taken from their souls by their deeds.
links.teaches: The eight qualities that the Kural gives to the one worshipped are, in the Jain hymn, the soul's own, lost to karma by those who will not praise, so the failure to worship costs the self what the god possesses.

gains.a: a source for the term, which shows the hymn reworking a couplet every Tamil hearer knew
gains.b: a Jain reading in which the eight qualities are the soul's nature, so the couplet's god is what the freed soul becomes

links.note: Tirumanthiram 444 gives the eight qualities (குணம் எண்குணம்) to matted-haired Siva who keeps the world; 1469 has them seized from souls by the robber deeds.
links.teaches: On my reading of 1469, the two texts disagree about whose the eight qualities are: for Tirumular they are the attributes of a God who protects, for the Jain hymn they are the soul's own and are lost to karma, with no protector named who restores them.

gains.a: a Saiva rival that sharpens the hymn's claim that the qualities belong to the soul
gains.b: a Jain counter-reading in which the eight qualities are not a divine possession but a human one under siege

links.note: In 1420 Civakan praises the Jina who teaches that the eight karmas (எண்வினையும்) pass through love and yet do not pass because of love; 1469 shows the eight qualities of the soul seized by those karmas.
links.teaches: The two hymns of this ilampakam make a pair: the eight deeds of 1420 are the robbers of 1469, so the reader sees what the soul loses before the paradox of love and release in 1420 can be weighed.

links.note: In 1456 Subhadran consoles the grieving mother that the man of merit will meet her daughter's eyes tomorrow (கண்ணுறு நாளை); in 1471 their gazes meet as Civakan enters the city.
links.teaches: The meeting of the eyes is the fulfilment of a precise prediction, so the first-sight love of the next verses is framed as a fate announced in advance rather than a chance encounter.

links.note: Kural 1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame; in 1472 Kemasari's inner restraint and modesty (உண்ணிறை நாணும்) break together at the first sight of Civakan.
links.teaches: The Kural's woman says this in separation as a confession of defeat; the epic makes the same breaking happen at first sight and treats it as the sign that the destined man has come, turning a lament into an omen.

gains.a: the frame of நிறை as a door with நாண் as its bolt, which explains why the two words break together
gains.b: a scene that moves the breaking of restraint from the end of a love to its first instant

links.note: Kural 1082 says her returned look is like a striking goddess (தாக்கணங்கு) bringing an army; in 1473 Kemasari's look becomes an afflicting goddess (நோக்கணங்கு) and Civakan wonders whether she is a தாக்கணங்கு or a mortal.
links.teaches: The Kural settles that the woman is human and keeps the goddess as a figure for her look; the epic stops at the doubt and stacks அணங்கு on lute, look and woman, so the hero's own art is made one of the goddesses that strike him.

gains.a: the term and its sense of a look that strikes back, which the verse expands in its triple pun
gains.b: a narrative moment in which the man's doubt is left unresolved and he sinks under it

links.note: In 1327 Civakan settles that Padumai is no goddess by three marks (her garland fades, her eyes blink, her feet touch the ground); in 1473 he asks whether Kemasari is a goddess or a daughter and does not settle it.
links.teaches: The hero who coolly tested a woman's humanity by signs in one ilampakam is in the next too struck to test, which shows the epic varying the same first-sight doubt from a clear-headed proof to helpless wonder.

links.note: In 1451 the astrologer foretells that the man at whose sight Kemasari instantly feels shy (கதுமென நாணப் படுவான்) will be her husband; in 1475 she looks at Civakan and turns her eyes away.
links.teaches: The averted glance is the very sign the astrologer named, so a lover's ordinary modesty becomes the proof of fate, and the reader knows the marriage is sealed before anyone speaks of it.

links.note: Kural 1086 says her eyes would not cause him trembling pain if her curved brows would straighten and screen them; in 1482 her brow is a strong bow bent at the middle that beats him.
links.teaches: In the Kural the brows could be the eyes' restraint if only they were straight; in the epic the bent brow is itself a weapon in league with eye, hair and breast, so the hope of a screen is gone.

gains.a: the idea that the brows might have held the eyes back, which shows what the epic's brow-as-bow has abandoned
gains.b: an extended scene of capture in which the brow joins the eyes as attacker

links.note: Kural 1087 likens the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes; in 1483 her breasts are bound by a bodice as cruel things must be bound.
links.teaches: Both treat the covering of the breasts as a restraint put on something dangerous; the epic adds that the binding fails, since the bound breasts still wreck her waist and him, while the Kural's cloth only warns.

gains.a: a reading of the bodice as a restraint on a dangerous force, which explains why the verse calls the breasts கொடியன
gains.b: a sequel to the image, in which the covering does not hold and the danger it marked comes to pass

new_concepts.gloss: music: song and the playing of instruments, as art, skill and power over hearers
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's words (பேரிசை வீணை 1466, கறங்கிசை 1461); id as declared in earlier Cintamani chapters

new_concepts.gloss: a blessing or wish spoken for another's welfare
new_concepts.label_source: the act of blessing in 1470 (பெறுக என உரைத்தாள்); id as declared in earlier Cintamani chapters

source_issues: 1461 and 1464: the physiognomic catalogue is compressed and several comparisons (குறங்கணி மயிலொடு, கெடிற்றழகு, மூக்கு ... தோட்டி) cannot be fixed with confidence from the verse alone.
1469 line 4 (ஓட்டிடுப வெண்குணனுங் கோட்பட் டுயிராவே): the construction, and so whose the eight qualities are, is uncertain.
1482 line 4 reads கொல்லுந் கொல்லுமே, with an unassimilated ந் before கொ; probably an edition or input slip for கொல்லுங் கொல்லுமே.
